Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01249

The human mind can understand what things are, but it cannot fully grasp pure existence itself, which is not one thing among others, as in God—exalted is His name—or pure nonexistence, which is not a thing in any way. It cannot grasp the first because it is complete and fully real; it cannot grasp the second because it is entirely lacking and unreal.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01250

Anything closer to God shares this condition in some way, such as the First Intellect and the intelligences that follow it. Anything closer to what is impossible likewise shares its condition, such as basic matter, motion, and things like them.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01251

In short, some things we know have the strongest existence: God, followed by the intelligences that do not depend on bodies and other spiritual beings. Others have such weak existence that they are close to nonexistence because they are mixed with it. These include basic matter, time, and motion. Between these two extremes are things such as material bodies, in the philosophers' view, and the bodies we form in imagination, in our view. We will explain later, when discussing the senses and what they perceive, that we can understand a body only by grasping its form apart from its matter in some way.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01252

As long as human minds are occupied with guiding these earthly bodies, they cannot grasp the first kind, just as bats cannot see sunlight because it overwhelms their eyes. They also cannot grasp the second kind, because these things have such weak and incomplete existence, just as sight cannot detect objects that are very far away or very small. The third kind, however, is within our power to know and understand: things such as distances, shapes, tastes, and colors.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01253

This is because most human souls in this world work mainly through imagination and the senses. What perceives must be of the same kind as what it perceives, just as food must be suited to the one who eats it. That is why these things are easy for us to know.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01254
Chapter — Can human beings know what things truly are?
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01255

Some books say that we can know composite things because we can define them by their constituent parts, but we cannot know simple things because their true natures cannot be understood. At most, we can describe them through their properties and effects. For example, the soul is said to be something that moves the body. What we know about it, then, is that it moves the body; its true nature remains unknown. The argument is that people disagree about what things are because each person notices a different property and judges the thing by it. If we knew the true natures of things, we would also know their properties, near and remote, because knowing a cause leads to knowing its effects. If that were so, no claim about the properties of a thing would need to be proved. That is the argument.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01256

Perhaps this writer has confused knowing an aspect of a thing with knowing the thing through one of its aspects. The first belongs in a statement about a concept itself. What is said there does not carry over to the things that fall under that concept, let alone to their properties or consequences. The second belongs in an ordinary statement about actual things. What is said of them applies directly to their real instances, but only indirectly to their accidental features and what follows from them. If a claim applies to one thing directly and to another only indirectly, that does not make it apply to a third thing, much less to anything further removed.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01257

We should also note that necessary connections between things arise from their actual existence, not from their abstract natures—except for features that belong to a nature simply because of what it is. What the mind takes from things in the world is their natures and concepts, not their actual existence as individuals. The intellect knows what a thing is; its actual existence is what brings about its actual consequences. So understanding a thing in thought does not mean that we also understand its consequences, whether near or remote. This resolves the difficulty.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01258

Al-Razi says in al-Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyya (Eastern Investigations) that simple natures can be understood. His proof is this: composite things must be made up of simple things, since every plurality contains unity. If simple things could not be understood, composite things could not be understood by definition. Nor could they be understood by description, since a description defines a thing through its properties. If those properties are simple, they could not be understood; if they are composite but their own simple parts cannot be understood, they too would remain unknown. In short, the same problem applies to the things those properties imply. So the claim that simple things cannot be understood would mean that we understand nothing at all, neither by definition nor by description. But that conclusion is plainly false, so the claim that leads to it must be false too. That is the end of his argument.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01259

There is a weakness here. Even if we can understand things made of parts, it does not follow that we must first understand each of their simplest parts. We need not accept that a definition of a composite thing requires knowledge of every part, down to the simplest ones; it may be enough to know its nearest parts, perhaps through a description. Nor must we know composite things by knowing their parts, near or remote. We may know them another way: not through their full nature or a definition, but through direct experience or a description based on their properties and effects. If asked how we know those properties and descriptions, we can say that we know them in some way, but not in their full nature. So the claim that simple things cannot be understood means that we cannot know their full nature, not that we cannot know anything about them—not even through general ideas such as “thing” and “possible.”
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01260

The right course here is to ask what “simple” means. Does it mean a simple concept, or a simple thing in the world? If it means that the intellect cannot know an individual real existence through a mental image that matches it, there is some truth in that, as we showed earlier in our discussion of existence. But if it means that the intellect cannot understand any simple concept, that is plainly false. The intellect understands existence, thinghood, and concepts such as “which” and “what,” among others. Whatever the intellect understands about a thing is either a simple concept or a composite one. If it is simple, it is either the full nature of a simple thing or one aspect of it. In the first case, the intellect has understood that thing’s full nature. In the second, it has understood that aspect, even if it does not know the full nature of the thing it belongs to.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01261

Otherwise, if every aspect had to be understood through another aspect, we would either go back forever or move in a circle, and so understand nothing at all. But that is clearly false. If what the intellect understands is a composite concept, it must contain at least one simple concept: a concept cannot be made from an endless series of concepts nested within one another. And even if the series were endless, there would still have to be a simple concept within it, since every multiplicity includes unity.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01262
Avicenna says in The Notes:
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01263

Human beings cannot grasp the true natures of things. We know their characteristics, the features that necessarily follow from their nature, and other features they may have. We do not know the defining features that make each thing what it is. We know that things have properties and accidents, but not their true natures. We do not know the true nature of the First, the intellect, the soul, the heavenly sphere, fire, air, water, or earth. Nor do we know the true natures of accidents. For example, we do not know what a substance truly is. We know that it is something that exists in its own right, rather than as a quality belonging to another thing. But that is not its true nature. We do not know what a body truly is; we know something with length, breadth, and depth. We do not know what an animal truly is; we know something that can perceive and act. Being able to perceive and act is not the true nature of an animal, but one of its properties and necessary features. We cannot grasp its real defining feature. That is why people disagree about what things are: each person notices something different and judges the thing by it.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01264

We identify a particular thing through one or more properties that distinguish it. Then, through what we first learn, we discover other properties of that thing, one by one, until we establish that it exists. This is how we reason about the soul, place, and other things whose existence we do not establish through their own natures, but through their relations to things we already know, or through an accident or a necessary feature. For example, we see a body moving and infer that something moves it. We see a kind of movement unlike the movements of other bodies, and infer that it has a particular mover or a special feature unlike the other movers. Then we follow its properties and necessary features, one by one, until we establish that it exists. That is the end of his argument.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01265

I say that we should understand Avicenna’s words as we have already suggested and shown in our discussion of existence. We can establish individual instances of existence only through indirect reasoning, in a way that resembles reasoning from cause to effect. We have explained that the true nature of any existing thing can be known in its particularity only through direct awareness. For us, the defining features of things are their actual forms in the world. We know them through concepts and descriptions that truly apply to them. These concepts may be part of a definition, which is made up of what are called a broader kind and a distinguishing feature. But they are not the same as the thing’s actual form of existence—the reality that makes it what it is.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01266

In some parts of The Healing, Avicenna says that the defining feature of an animal is not the concept “able to sense,” but the very soul that completes the animal’s nature, identity, and reality. The same is true of the defining features of other kinds of things. The first is the defining feature as we express it in words; the second is the feature as it exists in the thing itself. The feature itself is not what we say of the kind as a whole. What we can say is the idea drawn from that feature, which follows from the thing’s nature.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01267

This shows that existence has real instances outside the mind. It is not merely an abstract idea in the mind, defined by its relation to whatever it is applied to and multiplied as those things multiply, as later thinkers have claimed. Avicenna’s words here are almost direct evidence for what we have argued.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01268
Chapter — Different kinds of possibility
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01269

Possibility divides into what can exist in itself and what can exist in something else. Anything that can exist in something else can also exist in itself, but the reverse is not always true. Something may be possible in itself without its existence being merely possible for another thing. It may have to exist for something else, as forms do for matter and underlying subjects do for their qualities. Or it may be unable to exist in something else at all, like substances that exist on their own.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01270

Now, something that can exist in itself may or may not be able to exist through its own possibility alone. To explain this, we need to begin with a point we have already proved: every possible thing depends on a cause that is necessary in itself and necessary in every respect. Since this cause is necessary in every way, it cannot give existence to some things but not others, or to some things ready to receive existence but not others. Its relation to everything must be equal, and its giving must be universal and complete.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01271

Yet reason shows that some possible things exist before others in the chain of causes. We also see some events happen before others in a sequence over time. This difference in how things receive existence does not come from the Necessary Existent. It comes from differences in the natures of possible things and in the readiness of the things that receive existence.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01272

All possible things share this: each is possible in itself and in its nature. If that possibility alone is enough for them to receive existence from the Necessary Being, they must exist through direct creation, without being brought into existence at one particular time rather than another. Even so, their possibilities may differ in priority, how early they are, and in strength. The possibility of the Second Intellect is not like that of the First Intellect, since its existence is impossible from the standpoint of the Second Intellect. In truth, the Second Intellect’s possibility of existence is its possibility of existing after the First Intellect, just as the First Intellect is possible in relation to what comes after the Necessary Existent. The same applies to the other things brought into being. We will return to this question later.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01273

But if a thing’s own possibility is not enough for it to receive existence, then further conditions beyond its basic nature must be met before it is ready to exist. Such a thing has two kinds of possibility. One belongs to its nature: considered in itself, assuming that it exists or does not exist involves no contradiction. The other is its readiness to receive a particular kind of existence. This readiness comes only when the conditions are in place and the obstacles are removed. It is not quite right to say that this is a wholly different meaning of possibility, though the two kinds differ in what they apply to, as we will explain later when we discuss potential and actual existence.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01274

These conditions must come before the thing exists; otherwise, it would not be something that comes into being. For this readiness to form, there must be earlier events, with no first event at the beginning of the chain. There must also be something that keeps changing in its very being and identity, so that coming into being and passing away belong to its nature. And there must be a place for these events to occur. Through them, the thing becomes fully ready to receive what comes next. That place is matter.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01275
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01276
Chapter — Where the debate lies about making things, and the different views
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01277

There are two ways of bringing something about. In the first, a thing itself is brought into existence. This act concerns that thing alone, without joining it to anything else. Compound making is making one thing be something, or making it have a quality. Its result is a statement such as “the human being is wise,” which requires two terms: what is made and what it is made to be. Anyone who thinks compound making ultimately reduces to simple making—that only one thing is made, such as the relation of having a quality, becoming something, or being described—has missed the point.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01278

A relation such as becoming or being described is understood between its two terms. It helps us consider the terms together, or consider one through the other; we do not attend to the relation itself as a separate thing. So in compound making, the relation is included only as a subordinate part, not as an independent object. If we focus on that relation by itself and treat it as a thing in its own right, whether in the mind or outside it, we must ask a further question: does it need a maker in itself, or can it exist without a maker in itself but still need one to connect it to something outside its nature? Only clear proof can decide.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01279

The same distinction appears in mental knowledge. Forming an idea is one kind of knowing; it concerns what a thing is, whatever the thing may be. Judging a statement is another kind; it always requires two terms, a subject and what is said of it, with the relation between them included only as a subordinate part. Forming an idea brings the thing itself into the mind; judging makes the thing be something. Compound making applies only to qualities that come to a thing after it exists, when the thing does not have them by nature. It cannot apply to a thing and itself, or to a thing and its essential features, as in “a human being is a human being” or “a human being is an animal.” A thing’s being itself, or having one of its essential features, is necessary and does not need a maker.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01280

I do not mean that bringing the thing itself into existence, or bringing its essential parts into existence, does not need a cause. This is exactly where the followers of Aristotle and the Stoics disagree, though they agree that a thing’s essential parts cannot be separated from existence itself. Some theologians have argued otherwise; I have already mentioned some of their confused claims. Most of Aristotle’s followers hold that the first thing a cause brings about is its effect’s existence. Later thinkers explain this as the effect’s being existent: its nature is described as existing, in the sense we have already explained. They do not mean that the first effect is the relation itself, the caused thing’s nature, or existence itself. In their view, a thing’s nature as understood in thought does not need a maker.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01281

Another group of philosophers, known as the Illuminationists, says that the maker’s first and direct effect is the thing’s very nature. Once that nature is brought about, it is also existent; the maker does not separately give it existence or attach the relation “exists” to it. Those are ideas in the mind, and what they refer to is the nature itself that comes from the cause. The reality of a thing’s being itself is simply the thing; nothing else is needed. For example, once a cause brings about a human being’s nature, no second act is needed to make that nature what it is.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01282

Do not assume that because a nature’s being itself follows from the nature, and the nature is made, this relation also needs a maker. Nor, on this view, does the thing’s being existent need a separate act that first makes the nature itself. There is a difference between need that belongs to a thing in itself and need that arises only indirectly or by coincidence. A thing’s essential features and the qualities that necessarily follow from its nature do not need a maker’s separate action. They follow from the making of the nature, whether it exists or does not exist. If the nature is made, its essential features and necessary qualities are made by that same act. If it is not made, they too are unmade along with it. Just as eternal necessity removes the need for a cause, so does necessity that belongs to a thing’s own nature. The difference is that the first carries no dependence, even indirectly, while the second carries an indirect dependence. The maker brings about the nature of a human being, for example, and it is then human, animal, and able to learn by its own nature—not through a separate act of compound making.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01283

Nor is this because those features are made by the very same simple act, as al-Dawwani and his students thought the Illuminationists meant. When they say that a thing’s essential features are made along with its nature, they do not mean that a maker must separately make a human being human or an animal, or make those descriptions apply to it. They mean that bringing about the nature itself is one simple act. The act first brings about the essential parts; the nature follows, and its necessary qualities follow from it. The maker does not act on those qualities directly. The same applies to the view of Aristotle’s followers that existence is what is made: the nature becomes itself, and has its own essential features, without a separate act directed at each one.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01284

The fact that a nonexistent thing can be denied of itself means only that, on one view, its nature must be made, or, on the other, its existence must be made. It does not mean that the maker must act directly on it merely for us to point out a contradiction in arguments against existence being the effect. The early philosophers left no proof that settles either view. Each side seems to have treated its claim as self-evident. In their writings, we find only hints and brief indications.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01285

Some thinkers have argued that existence itself cannot be caused. Their arguments assume that existence is only an idea in the mind, something we add when we think about a thing. On this view, it is a thing's nature that begins, ends, comes to be, or disappears. We say that a human being exists or comes into being, not that existence itself does so. They therefore ask how existence alone could be what a cause brings about. With God's help, we have answered these objections in our discussion of existence.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01286

A later thinker offers another argument. If a cause produces only existence, he says, then every cause would be the cause of every effect. This is clearly false. His reasoning is that existence is one reality. If a cause can produce one instance of existence, why could it not produce any other?
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01287

Take water that becomes hot after being cold. The heat has a particular nature. Does its coming from the sources that give things existence require some new condition, or not? If it requires no new condition, the heat should always be there: the thing can receive it, and the source is always able to give it. But if a condition is required, does that condition belong to the existence of the heat, or to its particular nature?
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01288

Suppose it belongs to existence alone. If contact with water is a condition for coldness to exist, it would also have to be a condition for heat to exist, since both have existence and like cases must be treated alike. Whenever that contact occurred, heat would have to occur too: there would be something able to receive it, a source ready to give it, and the required condition. On the same reasoning, every event would follow from every condition. Particular events would no longer have their own particular causes and conditions. Experience plainly shows that this is false.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01289

The thinker concludes that the condition must therefore belong to the nature of heat, not to existence as such. And since whatever depends on something else needs a cause, causes must produce the natures of things, or both their natures and their existence—not existence alone. That is the end of his argument.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01290

This argument is weak in several ways. First, although existence is one reality, its levels differ in priority and lateness, in need and independence. We explained this near the beginning of the book. If existence were a general nature with many identical instances, the argument would have force. But we have shown that existence is not a general kind shared by many matching examples, nor a kind within a wider group or an extra feature added to things. The mind does draw from existence a general idea, like the word “being,” which it applies to things when it considers them. But that idea is not the reality of existence itself. The existence of each nature makes it distinct through that nature alone, without any extra feature. And yet the meaning of existence differs from the meaning of a thing’s nature, even though existence is one reality and the source of their differences. Seeing this distinction takes careful thought. Existence, simply as existence, can be a cause or an effect, a condition or something conditioned. The existence of a cause differs from the existence of its effect, and the existence of a condition differs from that of what depends on it. These are all different through existence itself, without any added feature.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01291

Second, the same argument would rule out the Necessary Being’s existence as the cause of the first caused thing, since the argument applies just as well here. Following that reasoning, if the Necessary Being’s existence causes the first caused thing, it must do so either because of its existence or because of its nature. The first option is impossible. Existence is one reality in the Necessary Being and in contingent beings alike. If the first caused thing could come from the Necessary Being’s existence, then it could also come from the existence of any contingent thing, such as an accident or a motion. But that conclusion is plainly false, so the premise must be false as well.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01292

The second option is also false, because the Necessary Being has no nature apart from its complete existence, beyond which nothing can be more complete. It does not help to say that existence is an attribute of the Necessary Being’s essence rather than identical with it. Decisive proofs show that existence cannot be an attribute of a thing in the technical sense. As we have already seen, existence itself is necessary in the Necessary Being and possible in contingent things: in the first it is independent and prior; in the others it is dependent and later. Being independent or dependent, and coming before or after, belong to existence itself. They are not features added to it from outside.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01293

Third, the claim that the nature of heat must exist forever if it depends on no condition or cause is neither sound nor well grounded. Those who say that a maker’s effect is a thing’s existence, not its nature, do not claim that the nature stands on its own without existence, and then serves as something that receives existence. In their view, only existence is real outside the mind. What we call a thing’s nature is united with that existence. The mind can consider each existence and draw from it a meaning that it then describes as the thing’s nature. Existence is what is described; nature is the description. Nature comes from existence as a shadow comes from the person who casts it, and a shadow has no separate existence. We have explained this more than once.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01294
Chapter — Refuting the arguments that a cause makes a nature existent
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01295

Some later thinkers argued for the view held by Aristotle’s followers as follows. What makes something need a cause is its possibility, and possibility is only the way existence and the like relate to a nature. So what first needs a maker, and what the maker first brings about, is this relation.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01296

They also argued that, since existence has been shown to be something added to contingent natures, those natures themselves cannot be what the word “existent” truly applies to. How could they be? This would be like treating a nature’s essential features as separate from the nature itself.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01297

They argued, too, that the priority of a nature to existence is not among the five familiar kinds of priority. It would have to follow if the nature itself were made. Finally, they argued that, although a thing’s denial of itself is always impossible, in contingent natures this is impossible only when we consider them as existent. We can say that a nonexistent thing is not itself, and a negative statement can be true even when its subject is absent. A contingent thing, considered in itself, does not resist nonexistence; in itself, it is not itself. The divine names include “O He, O who is He, O who is no he but He.” Until a thing exists, it cannot truly be said of itself. So what first and directly makes it need a cause is its being existent, not its nature.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01298

The first argument was answered by saying that possibility is not what most people take it to be: its meaning is more precise, as we have already explained. As for the second argument, it is indeed a thing’s nature that we describe as existent, but not in either of the usual ways. It is not like an essential feature, which applies when we consider the nature alone; nor is it like an accidental feature, which requires some further aspect to be added to the thing. Rather, the nature is described as existent because it has been brought about and established by its maker. This aspect lies outside what is being described, and is considered as a condition for the judgment, not as a limit on the thing itself.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01299

In short, before a nature has been brought about by its maker, none of its essential or accidental features can be truly predicated of it. Once it has been brought about, its essential features apply—not because it was made, but simply while it is in that state. Existence, by contrast, is predicated of it because it was brought about: through its maker and at the time it was made.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01300

The third argument is answered by saying that a nature’s priority to existence is another kind of priority, established by the proof. This is priority in what something is, rather than priority in time. A thing’s defining features also come before the thing in this sense and, in another sense, by the order of nature.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01301

The fourth argument is answered by saying that the fact that we can deny a nonexistent thing of itself does not mean that we can deny a contingent thing of itself without qualification. Not considering a thing’s existence does not mean that we are considering its nonexistence. And the fact that a thing is itself when it exists does not mean that it is itself only on the condition that it exists.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01302

The essential features of a thing are predicated of it while it is made and exists. Existence is predicated of the Necessary Being through its own eternal reality, without any condition of time or other qualification. In this sense, only God is the absolute “He”: He is only He. Predicating existence resembles predicating a thing’s essential features in one respect, and differs from it in another.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01303

In al-Mutarahat, Suhrawardi argues that natures are made by simple making. Since, on his view, existence is only a mental concept, a cause can be prior to its effect only by nature: the nature of the effect is a shadow of the nature of its cause, and the cause’s own nature comes first. A similar argument appears in another writer: we know directly that a maker’s first effect is the caused existent; but the caused existent must be a nature, since being described as existent, like other such relations, is only a mental consideration.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01304

An even stronger version was given by our revered teacher, may God preserve his honor and standing. Since a nature itself is what makes it true to say that something exists, consider what would follow if the nature, in its own constitution, did not depend on a maker. Then it would be existent in its own right and would no longer be contingent. That is impossible. So it must depend on a maker both in its basic constitution and in its being described as existent. In itself, in both respects, it is pure nonbeing, sheer negation, and pure potentiality. Its maker brings it into an established state by simple making; its existence then follows necessarily, without a separate act of making. These are our teacher’s words. We include them here as a mark of honor, in discussion with those who hold the opposing view.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01305

Notice that all their arguments rest on treating existence as a mental concept, like “thingness” or “possibility.” We have shown that particular existences are real—indeed, they are the truest realities—and that only general existence is an abstract concept of the mind, like the general idea of animality. We have already hinted at the difference, and it will become clearer. Once their starting point is shown to be false, the rest of their argument falls with it.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01306

Even if we grant that existence is only a mental concept, we still cannot grant that a nature itself is what “existent” applies to after the maker has brought it about. If that were so, the nature would no longer depend on its maker in order to exist. This would turn a contingent nature into something necessary in itself. For those thinkers, what makes something necessary in itself is that its own reality is the source of the judgment “existent.” What makes something contingent is that its own reality is not such a source. If, after its nature had been brought about, a contingent thing could itself be the source of the judgment “existent,” without our considering anything else or any other relation, then existence would belong to it by its own nature.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01307

It does not help to say that a thing has its defining features without any reference to a cause or condition, whereas calling it “existent” requires us to consider that its maker brought it about. The nature’s being made, or its connection to its cause, must either be part of what “existent” applies to or not. If it is not, the problem remains: a contingent nature would become necessary in itself. If it is, then what “existent” applies to includes both the nature and this relation to its cause. The maker’s effect would then include both the nature and that further aspect. In the sense explained earlier, this means that the maker brings about the nature’s having existence, as Aristotle’s followers hold.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01308

It is remarkable that al-Dawani, despite being so deeply committed to the view that a nature itself is the maker’s effect, writes in one of his notes that the Necessary Being is pure existence, standing by itself, and free in itself from all limits and qualifications. It exists in itself, has its own identity, knows in itself, and has power in itself. By this he means that the basis for predicating all these attributes of it is its simple reality, which contains no multiplicity at all.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01309

He says that other things are existent through something else: the maker brings them about in such a way that, when the mind considers them, it draws the idea of existence from them. They are existent because of the maker in this respect, not through themselves, unlike the Necessary Being.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01310

After a passage we have left out, he says: “This general meaning, shared by all things, is an abstract idea the mind uses to describe them. In reality, it is identical with neither of them. Yet the basis for applying it to the Necessary Being is the Necessary Being itself; the basis for applying it to anything else is that thing’s nature insofar as it has been made by another. In both cases, the concept applied is added by the mind. But in contingent things, the mind draws it from an aspect they receive from their maker; in the Necessary Being, it comes from the Being itself. As we have said, the Necessary Being is existence that stands by itself. When the mind considers it, it draws the idea of existence from it, unlike everything else.” That is the end of his quotation.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01311

In short, these thinkers say that contingent natures become existent in one of three ways. Existence may be added to them, as Aristotle’s followers are said to hold; the maker may bring about the nature itself, as Suhrawardi’s Illuminationist school is often said to hold; or the maker may make the nature related to itself, as some philosophers concerned with divine matters hold. These thinkers reject the first view, and we have shown what is wrong with the second. So they are left with the third: what is made is the nature’s relation to its maker. In other words, the maker performs a compound act, placing a relation between the nature and existence.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01312

Here is another way to refute this view. If a nature depended on its maker in its very constitution, the maker would be part of what makes that nature what it is. The maker would therefore come before the nature in the way an essential feature comes before the thing that has it—a kind of priority these thinkers themselves accept. It would follow that we could not think of a nature without also thinking of its maker and its relation to that maker. But we can. We can sometimes grasp a nature fully without considering anything else, let alone its maker, and say that a nature considered in itself is nothing but itself. This shows that natures and general kinds are not related to anything else in themselves. Their relation to something else comes from another aspect, whether that aspect is an idea drawn by the mind or something added in reality.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01313

This does not mean that a nature can exist apart from existence outside the mind, as the Mu‘tazilites claimed, or apart from it in the mind, as some Sufis are said to claim about the “fixed archetypes.” A contingent thing that has not come to exist is not anything at all, and firm proofs show that thinghood cannot be separated from existence. The difference is this: those thinkers say that a nature depends on its maker in its very self, while depending on existence only indirectly. We say that what makes it need a cause is its being existent—that is, its becoming something that can truly be judged existent—not its nature considered in itself. Neither view requires nature and existence to come apart.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01314

Another way to refute this view: the nature of a contingent thing is not particular in itself. If it were, it could not be general—that is, open to being applied to many things in the mind. Its becoming a particular thing must therefore come from something added to it. These thinkers hold that a thing cannot exist until it is particular. Careful thinkers say that it becomes particular through its own specific existence, whether that existence is real outside the mind or an idea the mind draws from it.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01315

The same general nature has the same relation to its maker in every instance we can imagine. Unless the maker determines it as one particular thing, it cannot be brought about. So what the maker brings about directly is not the general nature by itself, but that nature together with its particularity, its existence, or whatever we choose to call that further aspect. Someone might object that the maker itself makes the nature particular, without anything being added to it.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01316

But this works only if the maker’s effect is some form of the reality of existence, not a nature. A nature is a general idea that we can consider in itself, apart from its maker and everything else. If it were already particular and existent in itself, it would be necessary in itself, as we have shown. If it is not, then it is clear that it can become particular and existent in reality only by changing from what it was in itself. If it remained exactly as it was when it came to exist, it would not become particular or existent, even through another. The change must happen either by adding something, such as existence, or by newly relating the nature to something else. The first option is rejected by these thinkers; the second would mean that the nature itself turned into something else, which is impossible by its very nature.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01317

Another problem follows for those who say that makers make natures. Since they treat existence as a mental concept, the things that affect and are affected by one another would be natures alone, with existence left out. Then made things—especially everything except the first made thing—would be necessary results of natures. But, for these thinkers, a nature’s necessary result is only a mental idea and has no reality at all. Think carefully about this.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01318

A Throne-inspired reminder: Suhrawardi and his followers, following ancient philosophers such as Agathodaemon, Empedocles, Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, held that God, the intelligences, and the souls are luminous beings. Their light and existence are not separate from what they are. So we might understand Suhrawardi’s claim that existence is a mental concept to mean that only general existence—the familiar, easy-to-grasp idea—is mental. The particular existences, which are themselves levels of light, would still be real. We might also understand his arguments against saying that a nature is existent as arguments against existence being added to a nature from outside, not against particular instances of existence being real in themselves.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01319

But this reading raises a problem about light that belongs to another thing, rather than existing on its own. For Suhrawardi, light is one simple reality, and its different instances vary only in strength and weakness. At the highest level is the rich, self-sufficient light of the Necessary Being. At the lowest, light is only a feature of another thing, whether that thing is luminous or dark. Why could one instance of a single reality stand by itself while another depends on something else?
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01320

Or perhaps Suhrawardi’s aim is to debate Aristotle’s followers, as he often does, and then quietly point toward what he himself believes. If so, his view avoids the problem that later thinkers face when they say general natures are made. For him, particular luminous beings are like the individual existences described by Aristotle’s followers: each is an individual reality that can be known only by direct awareness of it, not by forming a mental picture.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01321

As we have said, being at a particular level is part of what each level of existence is. We cannot think of one level without first considering the level before it. Each existence’s connection to what comes before it is part of its very reality; we cannot understand it as disconnected from its cause. So to make such a being is simply to make its connection to the First Being. The two cannot be separated, either in reality or in thought.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01322

This is unlike general natures. We can think of them apart from other things because they may be found in the world or in the mind, and their meanings are different from either kind of existence and from their relation to God or to anything else. Their only connections are to their own essential parts, which are also general ideas. Even ideas that describe relations are not, by their own nature, related to their maker: the thing related and the thing it is related to stand alike in this respect. For this reason, we cannot judge that a nature exists unless we consider some aspect beyond the nature itself.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01323

For a general nature, possibility means that existence and nonexistence have equal standing for it—or that being made and not being made are equally open to it, so neither is necessary. But the possibility of luminous beings means that they depend on something else: if we ignored their maker, they would be nothing at all, neither existent nor a nature. Ignoring their maker would be like ignoring what they are. This is unlike general natures, whose meanings we can grasp without considering anything else.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01324

For the Illuminationists who hold to simple making, the basis for causation is that a thing is pure existence, as al-Talwihat puts it, or pure light, in the language of The Philosophy of Illumination. For them, the true maker is the Necessary Being: existence or light at its fullest, with no lack at all. As we have learned, existence is known only through direct awareness; the reality of light is grasped only through a direct connection in which it is present. If we knew any part of it only as a mental picture, its reality would be changed, as we have explained elsewhere.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01325

So, for them, the effects that are luminous beings are real, individual results of their makers’ simple acts, not merely ideas in the mind. This does not mean that a made being is only a mental result in both its real existence and its existence in the mind. That would follow only if the natures of its makers could be present in the mind, but we have said they cannot. This shows that there are two kinds of nature and reality. One is identical with existence: it is neither general nor particular in the sense of having an added feature that makes it individual, because, as the First Teacher says, its existence and its individuality are one. The other kind is different from existence and can be shared by many things. The necessary results of the first kind are real, individual beings; the necessary results of the second are only general ideas, with no existence outside the mind. The truth of this account becomes clear only after careful study of their views with a sound mind and character.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01326

It is also strange that most people who say makers make natures reject any difference in degree among instances of the same general kind or species. Yet they treat existence as a mental concept and say, openly or by implication, that the nature of a cause comes before the nature of its effect. If the cause and effect are both kinds of substance—for example, the Active Intellect and prime matter—they must admit that the cause’s substance comes before the effect’s substance. They are reluctant to accept this.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01327
Closer examination
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01328

The question of differences in degree can be examined in a way that clears away the doubts, God willing. Here is a teaching from the Throne: sound reasoning shows that existence itself is what the maker brings about through simple making. Natures themselves are not made in this way, since, considered in themselves, they have no relation to their maker. We have shown that anything insofar as it is caused is connected to its cause in some way, though the nature of this connection is hard to grasp. This is true whether existence has a nature that by itself requires a relation to another nature, with nothing between the two, or not. Someone might ask: why is the maker’s first effect not a nature’s being existent, as Aristotle’s followers commonly say—in the sense of a compound statement?
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01329

I say this view is mistaken for two reasons. First, the maker’s actual effect must itself be something real. But being described as existent, however we understand that description, is only an idea. It cannot be what the maker brings about. Second, although a thing’s having a feature does not depend on that feature’s existence, it does depend on the existence of the thing that has it. So the nature must already exist before it can be described as existent. If it exists through that same existence, it comes before itself, and we end up bringing about something that already exists. If it exists through another existence, we must ask about that earlier existence and its being described as existent, and the chain goes on forever. There is a reasonable version of the view: the maker’s first and direct effect is an undivided reality that the mind can analyze into nature and existence—that is, what a compound statement expresses. But once we analyze it, we see that existence itself is the direct effect, not the nature, since a nature considered in itself has no relation to anything outside it.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01330

It is now clear that what makers bring about directly is existence, and nothing else. The mind then finds in each of these existences general features drawn from that very existence. It draws these features from the existence and applies them without considering anything outside it or beyond the level that makes it what it is. These features are called essential attributes. The mind then connects them to existence and describes them as existent. This is what the careful thinker al-Tusi means in his book The Undoing of the Undoing: the existence of caused things comes before their natures in reality, but the mind considers it after them. So the objection that a feature cannot come before what it describes does not apply here. What is real first and foremost is existence; the mind then draws the nature from it in itself and applies to that nature the derived description “existent,” taken from existence itself. In truth, what describes the nature is existence in this derived sense; what comes before it in itself is real existence. On our view, existence and nature stand in the opposite order from the one most people assume. Think this through carefully.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01331

Something similar appears in the words of a careful thinker, who says that a power acts on a nature that is itself the existent thing. On this view, the maker’s effect is, for example, blackness itself—the thing that exists—not its existence, not its being described as existent, and not the relation by which it is described. The mind links blackness to a maker because it exists, not simply because it is black. We say, for example, “It exists because of the maker.”
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01332
We do not say, “It is black because of him,” or “It is an accident from him.” That is the end of the quotation.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01333

This would be sound if by “the existent” he meant real existence itself, existing through itself and not through some added feature—like a relation that is related by its own nature rather than through another relation added to it, or like other things of this sort. But this thinker does not mean that. For him, “the existent” is a simple, universal idea that applies to everything and is obvious to the mind. There is no doubt that something understood in this way is not an effect of a maker, since it is only an idea.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01334

Bahmanyar says in The Attainment: “When a maker gives existence, he brings about existence. Giving existence means giving its reality, not giving its existence, for existence has a reality and a nature. Every composite nature has a cause that makes it real, not a cause for the predicate ‘that nature’ to apply to it. A human being has a cause in becoming real and being constituted as a human, but no cause is needed for the statement ‘this is a human being.’ It seems that an existent with a cause must be composite, so that it can be caused. Also, a caused existent is possible in itself and therefore needs to be brought into actuality. By ‘caused,’ we mean that its reality, considered in itself, is not actual. Just as, when you think of a triangle, you necessarily think of its three lines, so when you think of a caused existence, you think of its cause.” That is the end of his words. There are several points here that support our position. First, the maker’s effect, and what follows from it, is existence in its simple reality; the maker affects a nature by giving it existence. Second, he states plainly that a thing’s being predicated of itself has no cause—not a new cause, nor a cause of its existence. Third, the reality of a caused thing is constituted by the existence of its cause, so that we cannot understand it without that cause.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01335
By “composite nature,” Bahmanyar means a contingent nature considered together with its existence, whether it is simple or composite in itself.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01336

A doubt and its answer: Someone might think that existence by itself cannot be caused, since existence is one single kind of reality. If a cause acted on existence alone, it would be a cause fit to produce every effect. For example, heat in water depends on a condition; otherwise, it would always flow from the separate source that produces it. If the condition affected only the existence of heat, and not its nature, then the condition for heat would also be a condition for cold, since cold and heat occur together in the same subject, water. So when water is present, heat would have to flow into it: its nature can receive heat, the source is ready to give it, and the condition is in place. The effect would then have to occur. This would imply that everything comes about—a claim that is plainly false, as sense and experience show.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01337

Once you have grasped the principles we have established, you need no further effort to remove doubts of this kind. Remember this, my dear reader: take care not to misunderstand the subtle arguments and fine expressions of the philosophers, or their hints at difficult ideas. Many people heard them say, “Substance is substance by itself, and an accident is an accident by itself,” but did not understand what they meant. They thought the philosophers were saying that these things need no maker or cause at all. That is not what they meant.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01338

The philosophers said this because, when they examined existences and their features and consequences, they found that existences are the subjects described and the things that bear those features. General meanings and ideas in the mind are all descriptions and consequences. They saw that, in thought and understanding, the differences among existent subjects come from differences in the features and descriptions that attach to them, whether essential or accidental. The features themselves differ because of their own natures and existences. These occupy different levels: some are more complete, others less; some are stronger, others weaker; some come first, others follow. God brought them about as distinct realities in themselves, not because of some further cause within them, but simply as they are.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01339

For example, black things and white things differ because blackness and whiteness differ. Blackness and whiteness differ by their own natures, not because of some further cause. Anyone who thinks there must be another cause for their difference will be led on without end. Blackness and whiteness differ in themselves, not through some feature within them, but through their own natures, which are identical with their existence. This is what the philosophers mean. They do not mean that blackness, for example, was not made by a maker or produced by a cause, as many people unfamiliar with philosophy have supposed. You will understand this more clearly later.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01340

A clarification, with a hint: An effect must be suited to its cause. We have established that the Necessary Being is existence itself and exists through its own reality. So what flows from it must be the existence of things, not their general natures, which have no likeness to Him.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01341

Ibn Sina says in one of his treatises: “The First Good is, by its very nature, open and manifest to all beings. If this manifestation meant that something else acted upon Him, then His exalted nature would have to be open to the influence of another. That is impossible. Rather, His nature is manifest through itself. Some beings, however, are unable to receive this manifestation, so He remains hidden from them. In truth, the veil is in those who are veiled: it is their limitation, weakness, and lack. His manifestation is nothing other than His own reality, for what He is in Himself can mean nothing other than His very nature, as the theologians have explained. His nature is manifest to them, and for this reason the philosophers called it a form. The first being to receive this manifestation is the divine realm called the Universal Intellect. It becomes a distinct reality by receiving His manifestation, just as the image in a mirror becomes an image when the person it reflects appears. It is close to this meaning when people say that the Active Intellect is His image. Be careful not to say ‘His likeness.’ This is the Necessary Being.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01342

“Everything affected by an agent is affected through an image that comes from that agent; every agent acts on what it affects through an image that comes from it. This is clear from observation. Fire’s heat acts on a body by placing its image, warmth, in it. The same is true of the other powers that produce qualities. A rational soul acts on another rational soul like itself by placing its image there: an abstract form in the mind. A sword shapes a body by placing its own form there. A whetstone sharpens a knife by placing on its edge the image of what it touches: the evenness and smoothness of its parts.” That is the end of his words.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01343

One of the mystics said that every caused thing is made up by its nature of two aspects: one that resembles and reflects its maker, and one that differs from and opposes it. If it resembled its maker in every way, it would be the maker itself, not something made by it; it would be pure light. If it differed from its maker in every way, it could not come from that maker either, since a thing’s opposite cannot come from it; it would be pure darkness. The first, luminous aspect is called existence. The other, dark aspect is called nature. Nature does not come from the maker, because it is the aspect that makes the effect different from its maker. It is therefore an aspect that the maker does not possess, and nothing can come from what it does not possess. If nature came from the maker, it would be the aspect of likeness, and another aspect would then be needed to make the effect different. The effect is related to its cause like a shadow to light: it resembles the cause in its light and differs from it in its mixture with darkness.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01344

The dark aspect in a shadow does not flow from the light, nor is it part of the light, since it opposes the light and makes the shadow different from it. How, then, could it come from the light? In the same way, the aspect called nature in a caused thing does not come from its maker. This supports the view that nature is not made or given by the cause. Nature is simply what makes a thing what it is, and what distinguishes it from its maker and from everything else. It is the dark aspect we have described, which plays a role in simple things like the role matter plays in bodies.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01345

Ibn Sina points to this kind of composition even in simple things in The Healing. He says: “What always exists through another is not simple in its reality, because what it has in itself is different from what it has through another. Its identity, as it exists, is made up of both. So nothing except the Necessary Being is free from what is potential and possible when considered in itself. The Necessary Being is the one true individual; everything else is a composite of two aspects.”
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01346

What a thing has in itself is its nature; what it has through another is its existence. Its reality is made up of these two aspects, as a body is made up of matter and form. For this reason, Ibn Sina ascribes potentiality and possibility to nature as he ascribes it to matter. There is still a difference between this kind of composition and the composition of a body from matter and form, just as possibility means different things in the two cases, as you will see later, God willing.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01347

Do not imagine that, by placing nature outside the realm of what is made, these philosophers have put it on the same footing as the Necessary Being and made it equally independent of a cause. Nature is unmade because it is beneath making: making requires some kind of realization, but being a nature involves no realization at all. As soon as a nature is realized in any way—even as something unrealized—it depends on a cause, because what is possible depends on its cause whether it exists or not. The Necessary Being, by contrast, is unmade because it is beyond making, through its complete reality and self-sufficiency. So how could something unmade because it falls below making be treated like something unmade because it is above making? Understand the difference.
Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence
passage-en-01348
Imam al-Razi was right when he said that the claim that natures are unmade follows from the question of absolute nature: considered in themselves, natures are neither existent nor nonexistent.
